reference.source: American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern / Ryan's Retina
clinicalPearls: The commonest clinically significant peripheral retinal degeneration predisposing to retinal breaks, more frequent in myopic eyes and often bilateral

Appears as sharply demarcated, circumferentially oriented, spindle-shaped areas of retinal thinning, usually anterior to the equator, often crossed by a network of white sclerosed vessels (the lattice) with pigment clumping and yellow-white flecks
Overlying the lesion the vitreous is liquefied, while at its margins there is exaggerated, firm vitreoretinal adhesion, and it is this combination that predisposes to tears

Two break types occur: atrophic round holes within the lesion, which are more common, lower risk and often seen in younger myopes, and tractional tears at the posterior or lateral margins during posterior vitreous detachment, which carry a higher detachment risk
Although common in the general population, only a minority of eyes with lattice ever develop retinal detachment, so routine prophylactic treatment of asymptomatic lattice is generally not recommended

Prophylactic laser retinopexy or cryotherapy is considered in higher-risk situations, for example symptomatic tears, the fellow eye of a patient who has had a retinal detachment, or before intraocular surgery in selected cases
Patients should be counselled about retinal detachment symptoms such as flashes, new floaters and a field defect and advised to seek urgent review if these occur
reference.pathophysiology: Lattice degeneration is characterised by focal thinning of the inner retinal layers with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous and abnormally strong vitreoretinal adhesion at the margins of the lesion. Sclerosis and hyalinisation of retinal vessels crossing the lesion produce the characteristic white branching lattice pattern, while disturbance of the retinal pigment epithelium gives the pigmentary changes. Atrophic round holes may develop within the thinned retina. The principal risk arises during posterior vitreous detachment, when dynamic traction transmitted to the firm marginal adhesions can tear the retina at the edge of a lattice lesion, allowing liquefied vitreous to enter the subretinal space and produce a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
additionalDifferentials: Other peripheral retinal degenerations such as snailtrack degeneration, paving-stone (cobblestone) degeneration and white-without-pressure
Peripheral chorioretinal atrophy or old chorioretinitis scarring
Retinal holes or breaks from other causes
Pigmented lesions such as congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
Peripheral chorioretinal changes of high myopia
additionalInvestigations: Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to examine the peripheral retina
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a wide-field or three-mirror lens to characterise lesions and their margins
Wide-field fundus imaging to document extent and to monitor over time
Examination of the fellow eye given the frequent bilaterality
OCT where available to assess associated retinoschisis or subclinical detachment
Assessment for a symptomatic break, including Shafer's sign and subretinal fluid, if new symptoms develop
redFlags: New flashes, a shower of floaters or a field defect suggesting a retinal tear or detachment
Subretinal fluid extending from a break
Tobacco dust (Shafer's sign) in the vitreous
A tractional tear at the margin of a lattice lesion, particularly during acute posterior vitreous detachment
reference.prognosis: Most eyes with lattice degeneration remain stable and never develop retinal detachment, so the overall prognosis is good. Risk is higher in high myopes and in the fellow eye of a patient who has already suffered a detachment, and outcomes are favourable when breaks are detected and treated promptly.
pitfalls: Over-treating asymptomatic lattice with prophylactic laser when the evidence does not support routine intervention
Failing to examine the full peripheral retina with indentation and so missing lattice or an associated break
Neglecting to examine the fellow eye
Providing inadequate detachment-symptom safety-netting to patients with known lattice
Assuming laser retinopexy abolishes all future detachment risk
